short: Fifteen years that turned a collection of warring kingdoms into a single administered empire.
full:
Qin destroyed the last of its rivals in 221 BCE and immediately set about making the conquest permanent. The old hereditary domains were abolished and replaced with thirty-six commanderies run by appointed, transferable officials. Weights, measures, coinage, the width of cart axles and the written script were standardised; the aristocracies of the defeated states were moved to the capital at Xianyang where they could be watched. The chancellor Li Si drove the programme, and in 213 BCE had privately held histories of the other kingdoms burned to remove any alternative account of the past.

The cost was enormous. Hundreds of thousands of conscripts were sent to the northern frontier walls, the Lingqu canal and the First Emperor's tomb. When he died in 210 BCE the succession was rigged by the eunuch Zhao Gao, and revolt broke out the following year. The last Qin ruler surrendered in 206 BCE and Xianyang was burned. The dynasty lasted fifteen years, but the Han that replaced it kept its administrative machinery almost intact, and so did everyone after.
